tool.name: CMake
tool.tagline: The de facto build system generator for C and C++ projects
tool.description: CMake describes a C or C++ project as targets with their sources, dependencies and requirements, then generates Ninja, Makefile or Visual Studio builds for any platform. It is what most open-source and commercial C++ uses, and what IDEs and package managers expect.

glossary.def: The file, one per project folder, in which you describe a project to CMake: its programs, libraries, source files and settings.
A tool such as CMake that doesn't build anything itself, but writes the instruction files for a build tool like Ninja, Make or Visual Studio.
In CMake, the part that writes the files for one particular build tool, such as Ninja, Makefiles or Visual Studio. You choose it with -G.
The folder (often build/) where CMake writes everything it generates: build files, the cache and the compiled results.
A small, fast build tool. CMake can write Ninja's build files, and it is the usual choice on every system.
In CMake, the file CMakeCache.txt in the build tree, where settings passed with -D and the results of searches are remembered between runs.
A CMake variable stored in CMakeCache.txt. It keeps its value between runs, and set(... CACHE ...) never overwrites an existing one unless forced.
A setting a CMake library target passes on to every target that links it, such as its include folders, definitions or its own dependencies.
A C++ library made only of headers, with nothing to compile on its own; in CMake it is an INTERFACE library.
CMake keyword: the setting is used to build this target and is also passed on to every target that links it.
CMake keyword: the setting is used only to build this target and is not passed on to targets that link it.
CMake keyword: the setting is not used for this target itself, only passed on to targets that link it. An INTERFACE library is a header-only library.
CMake's name for a folder in the build tree; each source folder processed has a matching binary directory where its generated files go.
A CMake setting such as Debug or Release that chooses how much the compiler optimises and whether it adds debugger information.
A CMake generator, such as Visual Studio or Ninja Multi-Config, whose build tree holds all build types at once; you pick one with --config when building.
A CMake target that stands for a library already built and installed elsewhere, usually created by find_package, such as fmt::fmt.
A CMake module that downloads a dependency's source while configuring and adds it to your build as if it were part of your project.
CMake's test runner: the ctest command runs the tests registered with add_test and reports which passed and failed.
A named set of CMake options saved in CMakePresets.json, run with cmake --preset name instead of typing every option.
A CMake expression written $<...> that is worked out while the build files are generated, so it can depend on the build type, compiler or target.
A named group of installed CMake targets (install(TARGETS ... EXPORT name)) that install(EXPORT) turns into a file defining them for other projects.
A numbered CMake behaviour change (CMPxxxx). A project gets the old behaviour until its cmake_minimum_required version says it accepts the new one.
A CMake file read before project() that says which compilers and system libraries to use, for example to build for another kind of computer.
Building a program on one kind of computer (the host) to run on a different kind, such as building on a laptop for a phone or a small board.
The name a Linux shared library records for itself, such as libgeo.so.1; programs store it and look for a file of that name when they start.
A list of folders stored inside a program where it looks for its shared libraries when it starts, before the system's usual places.

concepts.name: What CMake is: a build generator
concepts.summary: CMake reads CMakeLists.txt and writes the files for a real build tool (Ninja, Make, Visual Studio); you configure once, then build many times.
concepts.why: Understanding the configure/build split explains most of CMake's commands and errors.
concepts.body:
For a one-file program you can type the compiler command yourself. Real projects have hundreds of files and several libraries, and must build on Windows, macOS and Linux, each with its own compilers and build tools. CMake solves that: you describe the project once, in a file called `CMakeLists.txt`, and CMake writes the instructions for a real build tool on the current computer.

So CMake is not a compiler, and not quite a build tool either: it is a **build system generator**. It can write files for **Ninja** (small and fast), **Make** (the classic build tool on Linux and macOS, driven by files called Makefiles), and the **Visual Studio** and **Xcode** project formats used on Windows and Mac. Each kind of output comes from one of CMake's **generators**. The build tool then calls the compiler.

The workflow has two steps:

- **Configure** (and generate): `cmake -S . -B build` reads the project's source **directory** (another word for folder; `.` means the current one), checks which compilers are installed, and looks for the libraries the project needs, its **dependencies**. Then it writes the build files into the folder `build/`, called the **build tree**.
- **Build**: `cmake --build build` runs the build tool in that folder. You could call `ninja` or `make` yourself, but `cmake --build` works whatever the generator.

Always use an **out-of-source build**: everything generated goes into the build folder, your source files stay clean, and deleting `build/` resets everything. You can have several build trees for one project, for example `build-debug` and `build-release`.

You only need to rerun the configure step yourself when you change options. If you edit `CMakeLists.txt`, the next build notices and reruns it automatically.

Pick the generator with `-G`: `cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja`. Ninja is fast and the usual choice everywhere; without `-G` CMake picks a default for the system (Makefiles on Linux and macOS, Visual Studio on Windows).
concepts.code:
# project layout
#   hello/
#     CMakeLists.txt
#     main.cpp

cmake -S hello -B hello/build -G Ninja     # configure + generate
# -- The CXX compiler identification is GNU 13.3.0
# -- Configuring done
# -- Generating done
# -- Build files have been written to: hello/build

cmake --build hello/build                  # build with Ninja
./hello/build/hello                        # run the program

# edit a .cpp file: just build again, only that file recompiles
cmake --build hello/build
rm -rf hello/build                         # start completely fresh
takeaways: CMake writes build files for Ninja, Make or Visual Studio; that build tool then calls the compiler
Configure with cmake -S src -B build, build with cmake --build build
Keep builds out of source so deleting build/ resets everything
pitfalls: Running cmake . inside the source directory, which fills it with generated files that are hard to clean up.

options: Configures the project and generates build files in build/
quiz.explain: That's the configure and generate step; compiling happens with cmake --build build.

concepts.name: A first CMakeLists.txt
concepts.summary: Write the minimal project: cmake_minimum_required, project, add_executable and a C++ standard, then build and run it.
concepts.why: These four lines are the start of every CMake project you'll write or read.
concepts.body:
A minimal `CMakeLists.txt`:

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(hello VERSION 1.0 LANGUAGES CXX)
add_executable(hello main.cpp)
target_compile_features(hello PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
```

- `cmake_minimum_required` must come first. It states the oldest CMake you support and tells newer CMake versions to behave as that version did, so old projects keep working. CMake 4 refuses projects that declare a minimum below 3.5.
- `project` names the project, optionally gives a version, and says which languages it uses, so CMake looks for their compilers. `LANGUAGES CXX` (C++) avoids also searching for a C compiler.
- `add_executable(name sources...)` creates a **target**: something to build, such as a program or a library, with its own source files and settings.
- `target_compile_features(... cxx_std_20)` requires C++20 for that target; CMake adds the right option to the compiler command for each compiler.

Pass settings at configure time with `-D`: `cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`. They are stored in the build tree's **cache**, a file called `CMakeCache.txt` where CMake remembers settings, so later configures keep them.

List source files by name rather than using `file(GLOB ...)`, which collects every file matching a **glob pattern** such as `*.cpp` (`*` matches any name). A glob is evaluated only at configure time, so a newly added file isn't compiled until someone reruns CMake. Explicit lists also show reviewers exactly what's built.

Command names ignore upper and lower case (`ADD_EXECUTABLE` works too), but lower case is the modern habit.
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(hello VERSION 1.0 LANGUAGES CXX)

add_executable(hello main.cpp greet.cpp)
target_compile_features(hello PRIVATE cxx_std_20)

# main.cpp:
#   #include <cstdio>
#   int main() { std::puts("hello"); }
#
# $ cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
# $ cmake --build build
# [3/3] Linking CXX executable hello
# $ ./build/hello
# hello
takeaways: cmake_minimum_required first, then project(), then targets
add_executable creates a target from a list of sources
Prefer explicit source lists over file(GLOB)
pitfalls: Globbing sources and wondering why a new .cpp file isn't compiled until CMake is rerun.

quiz.q: Why list source files explicitly instead of using file(GLOB SRC *.cpp)?
options: GLOB is not supported in CMake 4
A glob is evaluated at configure time, so new files are missed until CMake reruns
quiz.explain: The build tool doesn't know a new file appeared; only a reconfigure re-evaluates the glob.

concepts.name: The CMake language: variables, lists, if
concepts.summary: Read and write CMake's own language: set and ${VAR}, lists as semicolon-separated strings, message, if conditions, foreach and functions.
concepts.why: Every CMakeLists.txt is a small program in this language; knowing its quirks avoids hours of confusion.
concepts.body:
CMake has its own small programming language. Everything is a **command call** `name(args...)`, and every value is a **string**.

- `set(NAME value)` sets a variable; `${NAME}` reads it. An unset variable becomes an empty string, silently.
- A **list** is just a string with `;` separators: `set(SRC a.cpp b.cpp)` stores `a.cpp;b.cpp`. `list(APPEND SRC c.cpp)`, `list(LENGTH ...)` and `list(FILTER ...)` work on them.
- Unquoted arguments are split on spaces and on `;`, so `${SRC}` passes three arguments. Quote it (`"${SRC}"`) to pass a single string.
- `message(STATUS "...")` prints during configure; `message(FATAL_ERROR "...")` stops.
- `if(cond) ... elseif() ... else() ... endif()`; operators include `NOT`, `AND`, `OR`, `STREQUAL` (strings are equal), `VERSION_GREATER_EQUAL`, `DEFINED VAR`, `EXISTS path`, `TARGET name`.
- `foreach(x IN LISTS SRC)` loops over a list, and `function(name args)` ... `endfunction()` defines a function.

Scope: a function call gets its own copy of the variables, and so does `add_subdirectory` (a later lesson). Changes don't reach the caller unless you write `set(VAR value PARENT_SCOPE)`.

`macro(name args)` ... `endmacro()` defines a **macro**: like a function, but its body is pasted in where it is called, so it has no scope of its own and its changes affect the caller.

`if(VAR)` versus `if(${VAR})` is a classic trap. `if` looks up bare names as variables by itself, so write `if(ENABLE_X)`, not `if(${ENABLE_X})`. True values are `ON`, `YES`, `TRUE`, `Y`, `1` and non-zero numbers.
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(lang LANGUAGES NONE)

set(SRC main.cpp util.cpp)
list(APPEND SRC net.cpp)
list(LENGTH SRC n)
message(STATUS "SRC=${SRC} (${n} items)")    # SRC=main.cpp;util.cpp;net.cpp (3 items)

foreach(f IN LISTS SRC)
  if(f MATCHES "^net")
    message(STATUS "network file: ${f}")      # network file: net.cpp
  endif()
endforeach()

function(add_suffix out suffix)
  set(result "")
  foreach(x IN LISTS ARGN)
    list(APPEND result "${x}${suffix}")
  endforeach()
  set(${out} "${result}" PARENT_SCOPE)        # return a value to the caller
endfunction()
add_suffix(objs ".o" a b)
message(STATUS "objs=${objs}")                # objs=a.o;b.o
takeaways: Every value is a string; lists are ;-separated strings
Quote "${VAR}" to keep a list as one argument
Functions have their own scope: return values with PARENT_SCOPE
pitfalls: Writing if(${FLAG}): if looks up names by itself, so the flag's value is looked up again as a variable name.

quiz.q: After set(L a b c), how many arguments does foo(${L}) receive?
quiz.explain: Unquoted, the list a;b;c is split on semicolons into three arguments.

concepts.name: Libraries and linking targets
concepts.summary: Split code into libraries with add_library (STATIC, SHARED, or by BUILD_SHARED_LIBS) and connect targets with target_link_libraries.
concepts.why: Real projects are a graph of libraries and executables; CMake models exactly that.
concepts.body:
Most projects are a few **libraries** plus one or more programs and tests that use them. Create a library target with `add_library`:

- `add_library(core STATIC a.cpp b.cpp)` makes a **static library**: its compiled code is copied into every program that links it.
- `add_library(core SHARED ...)` makes a **shared library**: one separate file (`.so` on Linux, `.dll` on Windows, `.dylib` on macOS) that programs load when they start.
- `add_library(core a.cpp b.cpp)` without a type: static or shared depending on the `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS` option, letting whoever builds decide.
- `add_library(core INTERFACE)` makes a **header-only library**: just headers, nothing to compile.
- `add_library(core OBJECT ...)` compiles object files that other targets use directly, without packing them into a library file.

Then connect targets: `target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)`. This does far more than add `core` to the linker command. CMake builds `core` first, links it into `app`, and passes on core's **usage requirements** to `app`: the settings anyone using core needs, such as the folders to search for its headers (include directories) and the libraries core itself depends on. Passing these on is the heart of modern CMake, covered next.

Always link by **target name**, not by the location of the library file. A target name lets CMake track the dependency, choose the correct file name for each system and pass on requirements.

It's common to give a library a second name with a project prefix, an **alias**: `add_library(myproj::core ALIAS core)`. Code that links `myproj::core` then works the same whether the library is built in this project or found already installed on the computer. A name containing `::` must be a target, so a typo becomes an error instead of being passed to the linker as some unknown library name.
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(shop LANGUAGES CXX)

add_library(core STATIC src/cart.cpp src/price.cpp)
add_library(shop::core ALIAS core)
target_include_directories(core PUBLIC include)
target_compile_features(core PUBLIC cxx_std_20)

add_executable(shop src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(shop PRIVATE shop::core)    # include/ and C++20 come along

add_executable(cart_test tests/cart_test.cpp)
target_link_libraries(cart_test PRIVATE shop::core)

# $ cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja && cmake --build build
# [1/6] Building CXX object CMakeFiles/core.dir/src/cart.cpp.o
# ...
# [7/7] Linking CXX executable cart_test
takeaways: `add_library` creates `STATIC`, `SHARED`, `INTERFACE` (header-only) or `OBJECT` libraries
target_link_libraries links and passes on usage requirements
Link by target name; provide a prefixed ALIAS like proj::core
pitfalls: Linking by a path like ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/libcore.a, which loses build ordering and usage requirements.

quiz.q: What does target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core) do besides adding the library to the link line?
options: Makes core build first and gives app core's public include paths and flags
quiz.explain: Linking to a target makes it build first and passes on its PUBLIC and INTERFACE usage requirements.

concepts.name: PUBLIC, PRIVATE and INTERFACE
concepts.summary: Attach include paths, definitions and options to targets with target_* commands, and control what propagates to dependents with PUBLIC, PRIVATE and INTERFACE.
concepts.why: Getting these three words right is what makes libraries easy to use and builds correct.
concepts.body:
Modern CMake attaches every setting to a **target** with `target_*` commands, instead of setting variables that affect the whole project:

- `target_include_directories(core PUBLIC include PRIVATE src)`
- `target_compile_definitions(core PRIVATE CORE_INTERNAL=1)`
- `target_compile_options(core PRIVATE -Wall)`
- `target_compile_features(core PUBLIC cxx_std_20)`
- `target_link_libraries(core PUBLIC fmt::fmt PRIVATE zlib)`

The word before each setting decides **who** gets it:

- **PRIVATE**: only for building this target. Inner details: `src/` headers, warnings, libraries used only in `.cpp` files.
- **INTERFACE**: only for targets that link to this one, not for itself. Typical for header-only libraries.
- **PUBLIC**: both. Use it when the setting shows up in your **public headers**, the ones users include: the public include directory, a library whose types appear in those headers, a required C++ standard.

The rule of thumb: if a user of your library needs it to compile against your headers, it's PUBLIC; otherwise PRIVATE. Passing on continues down the chain: if `app` links `core` and `core` links `fmt` PUBLIC, `app` gets fmt's include path too.

Avoid the old commands `include_directories()`, `add_definitions()` and `link_libraries()`; they apply to every target in the directory and hide which target needs what.
concepts.code:
# header-only utility: nothing to compile, only requirements for users
add_library(mathx INTERFACE)
target_include_directories(mathx INTERFACE mathx/include)
target_compile_features(mathx INTERFACE cxx_std_20)

add_library(core STATIC src/engine.cpp)
target_include_directories(core
  PUBLIC  include          # users include <core/engine.h>
  PRIVATE src)             # internal headers
target_compile_definitions(core PRIVATE CORE_BUILDING=1)
target_link_libraries(core
  PUBLIC  mathx            # mathx types appear in core's public headers
  PRIVATE Threads::Threads)

add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)
# app gets: include/, mathx/include, C++20
# app does not get: src/, CORE_BUILDING, (Threads only at link time for static core)
takeaways: PRIVATE: only this target; INTERFACE: only users; PUBLIC: both
If it's needed to compile against your headers, make it PUBLIC
Use target_* commands, not directory-wide include_directories
pitfalls: Making everything PUBLIC, which leaks internal include paths and flags into every dependent target.

quiz.q: A library uses zlib only inside its .cpp files. How should it link zlib?
quiz.explain: zlib isn't visible in the library's headers, so the targets that use the library don't need its include paths.

concepts.name: Project structure and add_subdirectory
concepts.summary: Organise a project into directories, each with its own CMakeLists.txt, and understand how add_subdirectory scopes variables and paths.
concepts.why: A clear directory layout keeps CMake files small and lets components be reused or extracted later.
concepts.body:
As a project grows, split it: the top-level `CMakeLists.txt` sets up the project and includes subdirectories, and each component directory defines its own targets.

```
project/
  CMakeLists.txt          # cmake_minimum_required, project, add_subdirectory(...)
  libs/core/CMakeLists.txt
  apps/cli/CMakeLists.txt
  tests/CMakeLists.txt
```

`add_subdirectory(libs/core)` runs that directory's `CMakeLists.txt` right away, with its own **variable scope** (a copy of the parent's variables) and its own folder in the build tree, which CMake calls its **binary directory**. Targets, unlike variables, are **global**: a target defined in `libs/core` can be linked from `apps/cli` as long as it's defined first.

Paths worth knowing:

- `CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR` / `CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR` the directory being processed and its build counterpart. A **relative path** (one that doesn't start from the top of the disk, like `include/`) in `target_sources` or `target_include_directories` counts from the current source directory.
- `PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR` the directory of the latest `project()` call; prefer it to `CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR`, which is the top of the whole build and wrong when your project is itself included by another.

Guard optional parts with options: `option(MYPROJ_BUILD_TESTS "Build tests" ON)` and `if(MYPROJ_BUILD_TESTS) add_subdirectory(tests) endif()`. Prefix options with the project name to avoid clashes when the project is used as a subproject.
concepts.code:
# ---- CMakeLists.txt (top level) ----
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(todo VERSION 0.3 LANGUAGES CXX)

option(TODO_BUILD_TESTS "Build the todo tests" ${PROJECT_IS_TOP_LEVEL})

add_subdirectory(libs/core)     # defines target todo_core
add_subdirectory(apps/cli)      # links todo_core
if(TODO_BUILD_TESTS)
  enable_testing()
  add_subdirectory(tests)
endif()

# ---- libs/core/CMakeLists.txt ----
# add_library(todo_core STATIC store.cpp item.cpp)
# target_include_directories(todo_core PUBLIC ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)

# ---- apps/cli/CMakeLists.txt ----
# add_executable(todo main.cpp)
# target_link_libraries(todo PRIVATE todo_core)

# $ cmake -S . -B build -DTODO_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
takeaways: add_subdirectory gives each directory its own variable scope; targets are global
Use CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR and PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR, not CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR
Prefix options with the project name, e.g. TODO_BUILD_TESTS
pitfalls: Setting a variable in a subdirectory and expecting the parent to see it; use PARENT_SCOPE or, better, settings attached to a target.

quiz.q: A variable is set inside libs/core/CMakeLists.txt. Is it visible in the top-level file after add_subdirectory(libs/core)?
options: No, the subdirectory has its own scope
quiz.explain: add_subdirectory creates a new scope; only targets and cache entries are global.

concepts.name: Build types: Debug, Release and multi-config
concepts.summary: Choose optimisation and debugger information with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE (Ninja, Makefiles) or --config at build time (Visual Studio, Ninja Multi-Config).
concepts.why: Measuring the speed of a Debug build, or shipping one to users, is a classic and costly mistake.
concepts.body:
Compilers can **optimise**: rewrite your code into machine code that runs faster, at the cost of slower compiling and machine code that is harder to follow in a debugger. CMake knows four standard **build types** that choose how much:

- `Debug`: no optimisation, plus extra information for the debugger (`-O0 -g` with GCC/Clang, `/Od /Zi` with MSVC). Use it to **debug**: find and fix bugs.
- `Release`: optimised, `-O3 -DNDEBUG` (so `assert` checks are switched off).
- `RelWithDebInfo`: optimised with debugger information, `-O2 -g -DNDEBUG`. Good for a **profiler** (a tool that measures where a program spends its time) and for shipped programs you may still need to debug.
- `MinSizeRel`: optimise for the smallest program, `-Os`.

How you choose depends on the generator:

- **Single-config** generators (Ninja, Makefiles) build one type per build tree: `cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`. If you set nothing, the type is **empty**, meaning no optimisation flags at all; many projects pick a default in their CMakeLists when the user didn't choose.
- **Multi-config** generators (Visual Studio, Xcode, `Ninja Multi-Config`) hold all types in one tree, and you pick at build time: `cmake --build build --config Release`. There `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` is ignored.

So `if(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE STREQUAL "Debug")` is wrong for multi-config builds. Express per-configuration settings with generator expressions such as `$<$<CONFIG:Debug>:...>` (covered later), which work for both kinds.

A common layout is one build directory per type, `build/debug` and `build/release`, which presets make convenient.
concepts.code:
# default to Release for single-config generators when nothing was chosen
get_property(multi GLOBAL PROPERTY GENERATOR_IS_MULTI_CONFIG)
if(NOT multi AND NOT CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE)
  set(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release CACHE STRING "Build type" FORCE)
endif()

message(STATUS "Release flags: ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE}")   # -O3 -DNDEBUG (GCC)
message(STATUS "Debug flags:   ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG}")     # -g

# single-config (Ninja, Makefiles): one type per build tree
#   cmake -S . -B build/debug   -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
#   cmake -S . -B build/release -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
#   cmake --build build/release
# multi-config (Visual Studio, Ninja Multi-Config): choose when building
#   cmake -S . -B build -G "Ninja Multi-Config"
#   cmake --build build --config Release
takeaways: `Debug`, `Release`, `RelWithDebInfo` and `MinSizeRel` set optimisation and debugger flags
Single-config: -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE; multi-config: --config at build time
An empty build type means no optimisation
pitfalls: Measuring the speed of a build configured without CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, which compiles with no optimisation at all.

quiz.q: You configured with -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, then ran cmake --build build. What do you get?
options: A Debug build, because multi-config generators ignore CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE and default to Debug
quiz.explain: Visual Studio is multi-config; you must pass --config Release when building.

concepts.name: C++ standard, warnings and definitions
concepts.summary: Set the C++ standard with target_compile_features or CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD, add warnings per compiler, and pass definitions to the code.
concepts.why: Every project needs consistent language settings and warnings, set in a way that works on GCC, Clang and MSVC.
concepts.body:
Two ways to ask for a language standard:

- Per target: `target_compile_features(core PUBLIC cxx_std_20)`. As a usage requirement it propagates, so anything using `core`'s headers is compiled as C++20 or newer.
- Project-wide defaults: `set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)`, `set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)` (fail instead of silently falling back) and `set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)` (use `-std=c++20`, not `-std=gnu++20`). Set them before creating targets.

**Warnings** are compiler-specific, so branch on the compiler. Keep them `PRIVATE`: your warnings shouldn't be forced on your users.

```cmake
if(MSVC)
  target_compile_options(core PRIVATE /W4 /permissive-)
else()
  target_compile_options(core PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)
endif()
```

Treating warnings as errors is great in **CI** (continuous integration: the automatic builds and tests that run on every change), but annoying for people building your release with a newer compiler. CMake's `COMPILE_WARNING_AS_ERROR` target **property** (a named setting attached to a target, 3.24+) can be switched off when configuring with `--compile-no-warning-as-error`.

**Definitions** become preprocessor **macros**, names set with `#define` that your code can use or test: `target_compile_definitions(core PRIVATE APP_VERSION="${PROJECT_VERSION}")`.

For many values, `configure_file(version.h.in version.h)` generates a header from a **template**, a file with placeholders such as `@PROJECT_VERSION@` that CMake fills in. A changed value rebuilds only the files that include that header.
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(app VERSION 2.1.0 LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)     # writes compile_commands.json for code editors

add_executable(app main.cpp)
if(MSVC)
  target_compile_options(app PRIVATE /W4 /permissive-)
else()
  target_compile_options(app PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)
endif()
set_target_properties(app PROPERTIES COMPILE_WARNING_AS_ERROR ON)

configure_file(version.h.in version.h)    # contains: #define APP_VERSION "@PROJECT_VERSION@"
target_include_directories(app PRIVATE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR})
target_compile_definitions(app PRIVATE APP_NAME="${PROJECT_NAME}")

# compile line: c++ -DAPP_NAME="app" -I.../build -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror ...
takeaways: cxx_std_20 per target, or CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD with _REQUIRED ON and EXTENSIONS OFF
Branch on MSVC for warning flags and keep them PRIVATE
configure_file generates headers from templates filled with project values
pitfalls: Setting CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD after add_executable; it only applies to targets created afterwards.

quiz.q: Why should warning flags be PRIVATE?
options: Your warning choices shouldn't be imposed on projects that link your library
They make the build slower otherwise
quiz.explain: PUBLIC or INTERFACE options would be passed on to the compile commands of every target that links your library.

concepts.name: Using installed libraries: find_package
concepts.summary: Find installed libraries with find_package, link their imported targets like fmt::fmt, and point CMake at them with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH.
concepts.why: Almost every project depends on other libraries; find_package is the standard way to consume them.
concepts.body:
`find_package(fmt 10 REQUIRED)` asks CMake to find an installed **package**: a library installed on the computer together with files that describe it to CMake. `REQUIRED` makes configuring fail with a clear message if it's missing. On success the package provides **imported targets**, usually with a `name::` prefix, which you link like your own:

```cmake
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE fmt::fmt)
```

Imported targets carry the include paths, definitions and further dependencies, so one line is all you need.

There are two search modes:

- **Config mode**: the package itself ships a file `fmtConfig.cmake` (or `fmt-config.cmake`), installed with it. This is what modern libraries provide, and what **package managers** (tools that download and install libraries for you) generate.
- **Module mode**: CMake or your project supplies a `FindXxx.cmake` file of CMake code that searches for the headers and library files. CMake ships these for common system libraries: `Threads`, `ZLIB`, `OpenSSL`, `CURL`, `Python`, `Boost` (newer Boost versions provide their own Config file instead).

By default CMake tries module mode first, then config mode. `find_package(fmt CONFIG REQUIRED)` forces config mode.

If a package is installed in an unusual place, tell CMake: `-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/fmt` (a list of folders where packages were installed), or `-Dfmt_DIR=/path/to/dir/containing/fmtConfig.cmake`. Package managers such as **vcpkg** and **Conan** work by installing packages and then pointing CMake at them, through a toolchain file or presets (later lessons).
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(fetcher LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(Threads REQUIRED)                # module mode: FindThreads.cmake ships with CMake
find_package(ZLIB 1.2 REQUIRED)               # FindZLIB -> ZLIB::ZLIB
find_package(fmt 10 CONFIG REQUIRED)          # config mode: fmtConfig.cmake from the install
find_package(OpenSSL)                         # optional
message(STATUS "zlib ${ZLIB_VERSION}, OpenSSL found: ${OpenSSL_FOUND}")

add_executable(fetcher main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(fetcher PRIVATE fmt::fmt ZLIB::ZLIB Threads::Threads)
if(OpenSSL_FOUND)
  target_link_libraries(fetcher PRIVATE OpenSSL::SSL)
  target_compile_definitions(fetcher PRIVATE HAVE_OPENSSL=1)
endif()

# $ cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$HOME/.local;/opt/fmt"
takeaways: find_package(Name REQUIRED), then link the imported target Name::Name
Config mode uses the package's own Config.cmake; module mode a FindXxx.cmake
Point CMake at installs in unusual places with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH
pitfalls: Linking ${ZLIB_LIBRARIES} and adding include dirs by hand when an imported target ZLIB::ZLIB exists and carries everything.

quiz.q: find_package(fmt CONFIG REQUIRED) fails although fmt is installed in /opt/fmt. What is the usual fix?
quiz.explain: CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH adds install prefixes to the places find_package searches for fmtConfig.cmake.

concepts.name: Bringing dependencies in with FetchContent
concepts.summary: Download and build dependencies as part of your project with FetchContent_Declare and FetchContent_MakeAvailable, and know when a package manager is better.
concepts.why: It makes a project buildable with just CMake and a compiler, which is ideal for small dependencies and test libraries.
concepts.body:
**FetchContent** downloads a dependency at configure time and adds it to your build as if it were one of your subdirectories. Its targets then exist in your project:

```cmake
include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(fmt
  GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt.git
  GIT_TAG 11.1.4)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(fmt)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE fmt::fmt)
```

Here the code comes from Git, the most common tool for storing a project's history; `GIT_TAG` names the release to use.

Good practice:

- **Pin** an exact version, so builds can't change by surprise: a release name, or better, the unique id Git gives every saved change (a commit hash), which can never be moved.
- Downloading a release archive with `URL` is faster than copying the whole Git history. Add `URL_HASH SHA256=...`, a fingerprint of the file's contents (its **hash**), so CMake can check it got exactly the file you expect.
- Add `FIND_PACKAGE_ARGS` (3.24+) so `FetchContent_MakeAvailable` first tries `find_package` and only downloads when the package isn't installed. Package managers can then supply their own copy.
- `FETCHCONTENT_FULLY_DISCONNECTED=ON` or `FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_<NAME>` let builds without internet, or with a copy already on disk, skip the download.

Trade-offs: the dependency is built from source in every fresh build tree, its options and warnings mix with yours, and two dependencies fetching different versions of a third library will conflict (the first declaration wins).

For a few small libraries and test libraries (GoogleTest, Catch2) FetchContent is great. For many or heavy dependencies (Boost, Qt, OpenSSL) use a package manager like vcpkg or Conan, with `find_package` in the CMakeLists.
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(cli LANGUAGES CXX)

include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(fmt
  URL https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt/archive/refs/tags/11.1.4.tar.gz
  FIND_PACKAGE_ARGS 11)          # use an installed fmt >= 11 if there is one
FetchContent_Declare(googletest
  GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/google/googletest.git
  GIT_TAG v1.16.0
  GIT_SHALLOW TRUE)
set(INSTALL_GTEST OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)    # options of the dependency
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(fmt googletest)

add_executable(cli main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(cli PRIVATE fmt::fmt)

add_executable(cli_test test.cpp)
target_link_libraries(cli_test PRIVATE GTest::gtest_main)
takeaways: FetchContent_Declare + FetchContent_MakeAvailable add a dependency's targets to your build
Pin versions; FIND_PACKAGE_ARGS prefers an installed copy
Use a package manager for many or heavy dependencies
pitfalls: Fetching a moving name like main (the latest code), so builds change silently whenever the library's authors push changes.

quiz.q: What does FIND_PACKAGE_ARGS in FetchContent_Declare do?
options: Tries find_package first and only downloads if it fails
quiz.explain: With FIND_PACKAGE_ARGS, MakeAvailable calls find_package with those arguments and falls back to fetching.

concepts.name: Testing with CTest
concepts.summary: Register tests with enable_testing and add_test, run them with ctest, and discover GoogleTest cases automatically.
concepts.why: A single ctest command that runs every test is what automatic build servers and code editors' test panels rely on.
concepts.body:
CTest is CMake's **test runner**: the program that starts each test and reports which passed. Two commands register tests:

- `enable_testing()` in the top-level CMakeLists (or `include(CTest)`, which also adds a `BUILD_TESTING` option).
- `add_test(NAME parser_test COMMAND parser_test --fast)`. When `COMMAND` names a program target, CMake fills in wherever the built program ended up.

After building, run `ctest --test-dir build`. Useful flags:

- `--output-on-failure` shows a failing test's output (set `CTEST_OUTPUT_ON_FAILURE=1` to make it the default).
- `-j 8` runs 8 tests at a time; `-R regex` and `-E regex` select or exclude tests by a name pattern; `-L label` filters by label.
- `--rerun-failed` and `--repeat until-fail:20` help with **flaky tests**: tests that sometimes pass and sometimes fail with no code change.
- `-C Debug` picks the build type when one build tree holds several (Visual Studio, Xcode).

A test passes when its command exits with status 0. Test properties (settings attached to a test) change this: `WILL_FAIL`, `PASS_REGULAR_EXPRESSION`, `TIMEOUT`, `ENVIRONMENT`, `LABELS`, and `FIXTURES_SETUP`/`FIXTURES_REQUIRED` for tests that prepare or clean up for others.

With GoogleTest, `include(GoogleTest)` and `gtest_discover_tests(my_tests)` register each `TEST()` case as its own CTest test, by asking the built test program for its list of tests. Failures are then reported per case and `-R` works on case names.
concepts.code:
enable_testing()

add_executable(calc_test calc_test.cpp)
target_link_libraries(calc_test PRIVATE calc GTest::gtest_main)

include(GoogleTest)
gtest_discover_tests(calc_test)               # one CTest test per TEST(...)

add_test(NAME cli_version COMMAND calc_cli --version)
set_tests_properties(cli_version PROPERTIES
  PASS_REGULAR_EXPRESSION "^calc [0-9]+\\.[0-9]+"
  TIMEOUT 5
  LABELS smoke)

# $ cmake --build build && ctest --test-dir build -j8 --output-on-failure
# 1/4 Test #1: CalcTest.Adds ......   Passed    0.01 sec
# 2/4 Test #2: CalcTest.Divides ...   Passed    0.01 sec
# ...
# 100% tests passed, 0 tests failed out of 4
# $ ctest --test-dir build -L smoke
takeaways: enable_testing() + add_test(NAME ... COMMAND target)
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure -j N runs them
gtest_discover_tests registers each GoogleTest case separately
pitfalls: Calling enable_testing() only in a subdirectory, so ctest from the build root finds no tests.

quiz.q: When does CTest consider a test passed by default?
options: When it writes no output to stderr
When its command exits with status 0
quiz.explain: The exit status decides unless properties such as PASS_REGULAR_EXPRESSION or WILL_FAIL change the rule.

concepts.name: CMakePresets.json
concepts.summary: Share configure, build and test settings in CMakePresets.json, keep personal ones in CMakeUserPresets.json, and run them with --preset or a workflow.
concepts.why: Presets replace long, error-prone commands, and code editors such as VS Code, CLion and Visual Studio understand them.
concepts.body:
Instead of telling everyone to type `cmake -S . -B build/release -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -D...`, put those settings in **`CMakePresets.json`** at the project root and save it with the code.

- **configurePresets** set the generator, `binaryDir`, cache variables (settings CMake remembers in its cache), environment variables and a toolchain file (a file choosing compilers; see the toolchains lesson). A preset can take over the settings of others with `inherits`, and hidden presets serve as shared bases.
- **buildPresets** and **testPresets** name a configure preset and add build targets, jobs or test filters.
- **workflowPresets** (`"version": 6` of the file's layout, CMake 3.25+) chain configure, build and test into one command.

Use them with `cmake --preset release`, `cmake --build --preset release`, `ctest --preset release` or `cmake --workflow --preset ci`. `cmake --list-presets` shows what's available.

Placeholders like `${sourceDir}`, `${presetName}` and `$env{HOME}` keep paths working on every computer. A `condition` can limit a preset to one operating system.

**`CMakeUserPresets.json`** has the same format for personal settings (local compiler paths, extra flags) and should be kept out of version control by listing it in `.gitignore`. It may build on the project's presets.

Code editors read both files and offer the presets in their menus, so the terminal, the automatic build server and every developer's editor configure the project the same way.
takeaways: CMakePresets.json holds shared configure, build, test and workflow presets
Run with cmake --preset, cmake --build --preset, ctest --preset or cmake --workflow
Personal settings go in CMakeUserPresets.json, not committed
pitfalls: Committing machine-specific paths into CMakePresets.json instead of CMakeUserPresets.json.

quiz.q: Which file should hold the path to your locally installed compiler?
quiz.explain: User presets are personal and ignored by version control, while the project presets are shared.

concepts.name: Generator expressions
concepts.summary: Use $<...> generator expressions to vary settings by configuration, compiler, platform or target, evaluated when the build is generated.
concepts.why: They're the correct way to express per-configuration and per-compiler settings that also work in multi-config builds.
concepts.body:
**Generator expressions** look like `$<...>` and are evaluated during **generation**, after configuration, separately for each target and each configuration. They're needed because some facts aren't known while CMakeLists.txt runs: in a multi-config build, the configuration isn't chosen until build time, and where a target's built file will end up isn't fixed until generation.

Building blocks:

- Conditions that yield `1` or `0`: `$<CONFIG:Debug>`, `$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:MSVC>`, `$<PLATFORM_ID:Windows>`, `$<BOOL:${OPT}>`, combined with `$<AND:...>`, `$<OR:...>`, `$<NOT:...>`.
- `$<cond:value>` yields `value` if `cond` is `1`, otherwise nothing; `$<IF:cond,a,b>` picks one.
- Information: `$<TARGET_FILE:app>` the built file's path, `$<TARGET_FILE_DIR:app>`, `$<TARGET_PROPERTY:tgt,prop>`.
- `$<BUILD_INTERFACE:...>` and `$<INSTALL_INTERFACE:...>` give different values when a target is used from the build tree or after installation.

Many conditions accept lists: `$<CONFIG:Debug,RelWithDebInfo>` (3.19+) and `$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:GNU,Clang>`.

Because evaluation happens later, `message()` prints the literal `$<...>` text. To inspect results, use `file(GENERATE OUTPUT dbg.txt CONTENT "...")`. Keep expressions small; deeply nested ones become unreadable fast, and a helper variable holding a part helps.
concepts.code:
add_executable(app main.cpp)

target_compile_definitions(app PRIVATE
  $<$<CONFIG:Debug>:APP_DEBUG=1>                 # only in Debug builds
  APP_PLATFORM="$<PLATFORM_ID>")                  # "Linux", "Windows", ...

set(gcc_like "$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:GNU,Clang,AppleClang>")
target_compile_options(app PRIVATE
  "$<${gcc_like}:-Wall;-Wextra>"                  # quoted: no spaces inside a genex
  $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:MSVC>:/W4>
  $<$<AND:${gcc_like},$<CONFIG:Debug>>:-fsanitize=address>)
target_link_options(app PRIVATE
  $<$<AND:${gcc_like},$<CONFIG:Debug>>:-fsanitize=address>)

# copy a data file next to the built executable, wherever it ends up
add_custom_command(TARGET app POST_BUILD
  COMMAND ${CMAKE_COMMAND} -E copy_if_different
          ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/config.json $<TARGET_FILE_DIR:app>)

file(GENERATE OUTPUT genex-$<CONFIG>.txt CONTENT "file: $<TARGET_FILE:app>\n")
takeaways: $<cond:value> inserts value when cond is true for this target and configuration
Use $<CONFIG:...> instead of if(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE) so multi-config works
message() can't show them; use file(GENERATE) to see their results
pitfalls: Putting a space-separated list inside a genex without quoting, which splits the expression into broken pieces.

quiz.q: Why use $<$<CONFIG:Debug>:-DTRACE> instead of if(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE STREQUAL Debug)?
options: With multi-config generators the configuration is chosen at build time, after if() has run
quiz.explain: The genex is evaluated per configuration during generation, so it works for single- and multi-config generators.

concepts.name: Installing and exporting a package
concepts.summary: Install targets and headers with install(), export them with a namespace and write the Config files that let others find_package your library.
concepts.why: A library that installs a proper CMake package is trivially consumable by other projects and package managers.
concepts.body:
`install()` rules describe what `cmake --install build --prefix /usr/local` copies. For a library to be usable by others via `find_package(mylib)` you need four pieces:

- **Targets** with an export set: `install(TARGETS mylib EXPORT mylibTargets ...)`. `include(GNUInstallDirs)` provides standard destinations like `CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR` and `CMAKE_INSTALL_INCLUDEDIR`.
- **Headers**: `install(DIRECTORY include/ DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_INCLUDEDIR})`, or the `FILE_SET HEADERS` feature (3.23+), which installs headers declared with `target_sources`.
- **The export file**: `install(EXPORT mylibTargets NAMESPACE mylib:: DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR}/cmake/mylib)` writes `mylibTargets.cmake`, which recreates `mylib::mylib` as an imported target with its usage requirements.
- **Config and version files**: a small `mylibConfig.cmake` that includes the targets file (and calls `find_dependency` for public dependencies), plus a version file generated by `write_basic_package_version_file` from `CMakePackageConfigHelpers`.

Include directories must differ between the build tree and the installed tree, hence `$<BUILD_INTERFACE:${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include>` and `$<INSTALL_INTERFACE:include>`. Never put full paths into your source folder in the installed settings: CMake rejects them.

Test the result by installing to a temporary prefix and building a tiny consumer project with `-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` pointing at it.
concepts.code:
include(GNUInstallDirs)
include(CMakePackageConfigHelpers)

add_library(geo src/geo.cpp)
add_library(geo::geo ALIAS geo)
target_include_directories(geo PUBLIC
  $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include>
  $<INSTALL_INTERFACE:${CMAKE_INSTALL_INCLUDEDIR}>)

install(TARGETS geo EXPORT geoTargets)
install(DIRECTORY include/ DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_INCLUDEDIR})
install(EXPORT geoTargets NAMESPACE geo::
        DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR}/cmake/geo)

file(WRITE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/geoConfig.cmake
     "include(\"\${CMAKE_CURRENT_LIST_DIR}/geoTargets.cmake\")\n")
write_basic_package_version_file(geoConfigVersion.cmake
  VERSION ${PROJECT_VERSION} COMPATIBILITY SameMajorVersion)
install(FILES ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/geoConfig.cmake
              ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/geoConfigVersion.cmake
        DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR}/cmake/geo)

# $ cmake --install build --prefix /tmp/geo-install
# consumer: find_package(geo 1.0 REQUIRED)  +  target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE geo::geo)
takeaways: install(TARGETS ... EXPORT) + install(EXPORT ... NAMESPACE) create importable targets
Use BUILD_INTERFACE / INSTALL_INTERFACE for include paths
Ship a Config and ConfigVersion file so find_package works
pitfalls: Hard-coding absolute include paths into the exported target, which breaks as soon as the package is relocated.

quiz.q: What does install(EXPORT geoTargets NAMESPACE geo:: ...) produce?
options: A copy of the source code
A CMake file that defines the imported target geo::geo for consumers
quiz.explain: The export file recreates the installed targets, with their usage requirements, as imported targets.

concepts.name: Configure, generate, cache and policies
concepts.summary: Know what happens in each CMake phase, how CMakeCache.txt and cache variables keep settings between runs, and how policies keep old projects working.
concepts.why: Mysterious 'my change has no effect' problems are almost always about the cache or a policy.
concepts.body:
A CMake run has distinct phases:

- **Configure**: the CMake language runs top to bottom. Commands like `find_package` and `try_compile` probe the system; targets and properties are recorded. `message()` output appears here.
- **Generate**: generator expressions are evaluated per target and configuration, and the native build files are written.
- **Build**: the native tool runs; CMake itself is involved only to re-run configure when a CMakeLists.txt changes, or for custom commands.

The **cache** (`build/CMakeCache.txt`) stores settings that persist between runs: everything passed with `-D`, `option()` values, and results of searches such as `find_library`. A **cache variable** (`set(X value CACHE STRING "doc")`) is only written if it doesn't already exist, so editing its default in CMakeLists.txt has **no effect** on an existing build tree. Change it with `-D`, `ccmake`/`cmake-gui`, or delete the cache (`cmake --fresh` in 3.24+). A normal variable with the same name shadows the cache entry in that scope.

**Policies** keep old projects working on new CMake versions. When CMake changes behaviour, it adds a policy `CMPxxxx`; projects get the old behaviour until they declare a minimum version that includes the new one. `cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25...4.1)` means "works with 3.25, and uses new behaviour up to 4.1". Warnings about unset policies are hints to raise that range, not noise to suppress.
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25...4.1)
project(cachedemo LANGUAGES NONE)

set(GREETING "hello" CACHE STRING "Greeting to print")   # only if not cached yet
option(USE_FAST_PATH "Enable the fast path" OFF)
message(STATUS "GREETING=${GREETING} USE_FAST_PATH=${USE_FAST_PATH}")

cmake_policy(GET CMP0135 p)          # DOWNLOAD_EXTRACT_TIMESTAMP behaviour
message(STATUS "CMP0135 is ${p}")    # NEW, because 3.25 > 3.24 introduced it

# $ cmake -S . -B build                      -> GREETING=hello USE_FAST_PATH=OFF
#   (edit the default to "hi" in CMakeLists.txt)
# $ cmake -S . -B build                      -> GREETING=hello   (cache wins!)
# $ cmake -S . -B build -DGREETING=hey       -> GREETING=hey
# $ cmake -S . -B build --fresh              -> GREETING=hi      (cache discarded)
# $ cmake -L -N build | grep GREETING        -> GREETING:STRING=hi
takeaways: Configure runs the CMake code, generate evaluates genexes and writes build files
Cache variables keep their first value; change them with -D or --fresh
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION min...max) sets the policy behaviour
pitfalls: Editing a cache variable's default in CMakeLists.txt and expecting existing build trees to pick it up.

quiz.q: You change set(OPT ON CACHE BOOL "") to OFF and reconfigure an existing build. What is OPT?
options: ON, because the cached value is kept
quiz.explain: set(... CACHE ...) doesn't overwrite an existing cache entry unless FORCE is used.

concepts.name: Toolchain files and cross-compiling
concepts.summary: Describe a target platform in a toolchain file (compilers, sysroot, search modes) to cross-compile, and understand how package managers hook in the same way.
concepts.why: Embedded, mobile and multi-architecture builds all rely on toolchain files, and so do vcpkg and Conan.
concepts.body:
A **toolchain file** is a file of CMake code read before the first `project()` call, passed with `--toolchain file.cmake` (or `-DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=...`). It describes the **target** system the program will run on, as opposed to the **host**, the computer running the build. Building for a different kind of computer than your own is **cross-compiling**:

- `CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME` (`Linux`, `Windows`, `Android`, `Generic` for bare metal) and `CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR`. Setting `CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME` is what tells CMake it is cross-compiling (`CMAKE_CROSSCOMPILING` becomes true).
- `CMAKE_C_COMPILER` / `CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER`, for example `aarch64-linux-gnu-g++`.
- `CMAKE_SYSROOT`: the target's headers and libraries.
- `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH` and the `CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_*` variables: search for libraries, headers and packages only in the target root, but for programs (code generators, tools) on the host.

Because the compiler is fixed at the first configure, switching toolchains requires a fresh build directory.

Things that break when cross-compiling: running freshly built executables during the build (code generators must be built for the host, or found as host tools), `try_run` checks, and tests (use `CMAKE_CROSSCOMPILING_EMULATOR`, e.g. `qemu-aarch64`, to run them).

Package managers use the same hook: **vcpkg** provides `scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake` as a toolchain that installs dependencies and adds them to the search path, and **Conan** generates `conan_toolchain.cmake`. A toolchain file can chain to another via `include()`.
concepts.code:
# aarch64-linux.cmake  (use: cmake -S . -B build-arm --toolchain aarch64-linux.cmake)
set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME Linux)
set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR aarch64)

set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER   aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc)
set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER aarch64-linux-gnu-g++)
set(CMAKE_SYSROOT /opt/sysroots/aarch64)

# libraries, headers and packages from the target; programs from the host
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PROGRAM NEVER)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_LIBRARY ONLY)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_INCLUDE ONLY)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PACKAGE ONLY)

# run target binaries (tests, gtest discovery) through an emulator
set(CMAKE_CROSSCOMPILING_EMULATOR qemu-aarch64;-L;/opt/sysroots/aarch64)

# vcpkg instead:  cmake -S . -B build --toolchain $VCPKG_ROOT/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake
takeaways: A toolchain file describes the target system and is loaded before project()
CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME turns on cross-compiling; FIND_ROOT_PATH modes separate host and target
vcpkg and Conan integrate through toolchain files too
pitfalls: Reusing a build directory after changing toolchain files; the compiler is cached at first configure, so start fresh.

quiz.q: Why set CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PROGRAM to NEVER when cross-compiling?
options: Build-time tools like code generators must run on the host, so they shouldn't be searched in the target sysroot
Programs can't be found in a sysroot
quiz.explain: Programs run during the build on the host machine, while libraries and headers must come from the target.

concepts.name: Shared libraries, symbol visibility and RPATH
concepts.summary: Hide symbols by default with GenerateExportHeader, set VERSION and SOVERSION, and make installed programs find their libraries via RPATH.
concepts.why: Shared-library details decide whether your programs run after installation and whether your ABI stays stable.
concepts.body:
Shared libraries add concerns static ones don't have.

**Symbol visibility.** On Linux every function is exported by default; on Windows nothing is unless marked `__declspec(dllexport)`. Make both behave the same by hiding symbols by default and exporting your **API** (application programming interface: the functions and classes others may call) explicitly:

- `set_target_properties(geo PROPERTIES CXX_VISIBILITY_PRESET hidden VISIBILITY_INLINES_HIDDEN ON)`
- `include(GenerateExportHeader)` and `generate_export_header(geo)` create `geo_export.h` with a `GEO_EXPORT` macro to put on public classes and functions.

Smaller export tables load faster, avoid symbol clashes and make ABI breakage visible.

**Versioning.** `VERSION 1.4.2` and `SOVERSION 1` properties produce `libgeo.so.1.4.2`. Its **SONAME**, the name programs record and look for when they start, is `libgeo.so.1`, and CMake adds **symbolic links** (small files that point to another file) with the shorter names. Bump SOVERSION only when you break the ABI.

**Finding libraries when a program starts.** An executable records an **RPATH** listing directories to search. CMake gives build-tree binaries an RPATH pointing at the build tree, and by default **strips** it at install time, so installed programs may fail with "cannot open shared object file". Set `CMAKE_INSTALL_RPATH` to a path that starts from the program's own folder, `$ORIGIN/../lib` on Linux or `@loader_path/../lib` on macOS, to make the installed tree relocatable. Windows has no RPATH: DLLs must sit next to the executable or in a folder listed in `PATH` (the list of folders Windows searches), which `$<TARGET_RUNTIME_DLLS:app>` (3.21+) helps copy.
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(geo VERSION 1.4.2 LANGUAGES CXX)
include(GNUInstallDirs)
include(GenerateExportHeader)

add_library(geo SHARED src/geo.cpp)
generate_export_header(geo)                 # writes geo_export.h with GEO_EXPORT
target_include_directories(geo PUBLIC
  "$<BUILD_INTERFACE:${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include;${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}>")
set_target_properties(geo PROPERTIES
  CXX_VISIBILITY_PRESET hidden
  VISIBILITY_INLINES_HIDDEN ON
  VERSION ${PROJECT_VERSION}                # libgeo.so.1.4.2
  SOVERSION ${PROJECT_VERSION_MAJOR})       # SONAME libgeo.so.1

add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE geo)
set_target_properties(app PROPERTIES INSTALL_RPATH "$ORIGIN/../${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR}")
install(TARGETS geo app)

# include/geo.h:  #include "geo_export.h"
#                 GEO_EXPORT double area(double r);   // exported; helpers stay hidden
# $ readelf -d build/libgeo.so | grep SONAME   -> [libgeo.so.1]
takeaways: Hide symbols by default and export the API with generate_export_header
VERSION and SOVERSION set file names and the SONAME
Set INSTALL_RPATH to $ORIGIN/../lib so installed binaries find their libraries
pitfalls: Installing a program linked to your shared library without an install RPATH, so it only runs from the build tree.

quiz.q: An installed executable fails with 'error while loading shared libraries: libgeo.so.1'. It ran fine from the build directory. Why?
options: CMake removed the build-tree RPATH at install time and no install RPATH was set
quiz.explain: Build-tree binaries get an RPATH to the build directory; installed ones need CMAKE_INSTALL_RPATH or INSTALL_RPATH.
